title: China’s gallium, germanium reprieve gives US time, not certainty
author: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
text: China has extended its suspension of a ban on gallium and germanium exports to the US to 27 January 2027, keeping a licensed route open for non-military US buyers but setting another deadline for the new year.China’s Ministry of Commerce announced the extension on 24 November, three days before the pause was due to lapse. The first suspension, agreed after the Trump–Xi meeting in Busan, lasted a year; the shorter window closely reflects China’s rare earth pause, extended to 10 January. Exports to US military end users remain banned, and every shipment still needs a licence, as it has since August 2023.Gallium metal (99.99%, CIF Europe) fell 9% to $3,150/kg on 26 November from $3,450/kg two weeks earlier, as assessed by Benchmark’s Gallium and Germanium Price Assessments, but remains ~2.8 times the Q4 2025 ex-China average. Prices had already started to soften before the announcement, and the extension has done little to change sentiment. Germanium metal (99.999%, CIF Europe) held at $15,500/kg, ~2.7 times its average price in Q4 2025.“This is a reprieve for non-military consumers in the US, but the volumes reaching them have been small since the ban was first suspended, and a two-month extension is unlikely to move the needle,” said Mike Finch, Head of Strategic Initiatives at Benchmark. “It does nothing for long-term confidence in supply security, so diversifying supply chains and procurement options will stay at the front of buyers’ minds, whatever Beijing decides in January.”The metal exists but is not reaching the USChina’s unwrought gallium exports fell 94% in 2025 and had not recovered in early 2026, while recorded shipments to the US have been close to zero since 2023.“I see little to no impact from this. The US has not received any Ga or Ge [in] over three years, and any licence attempt has either failed on the US side due to compliance reasons or due to Chinese restrictions on military uses,” a Europe-based minor metals trader told Benchmark.Benchmark’s Gallium Service puts China’s 2026 surplus at 275t against an ex-China shortfall of 182t, before trade. Its Germanium Service shows the same pattern, with a 53t Chinese surplus against a 52t ex-China gap. Both base cases assume licensing continues at 2026 export volumes throughout next year.Diversification is under way, but slowlyEx-China primary gallium supply is forecast to rise from 10t in 2026 to more than 200t by 2030, supported by government money such as the US Department of War’s $400m commitment to Atalco’s Louisiana project. Ex-China primary germanium supply almost doubles, from 45t to 84t. Even so, both markets will still remain reliant on Chinese material, albeit to a lesser extent, into the next decade.To learn more about Benchmark’s gallium and germanium prices and forecasts, fill out the form below and one of the team will be in touch.
